title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
Experiments are one of the main ways in which we expand our understanding of biology. In this hands-on course, students will develop fundamental skills in experimental design, data analysis, and visualization. Students will also learn how to use the coding language R to analyze and visualize data. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe experimental designs and analytic techniques (t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression, mixed effects models, etc.) commonly used in biological research. Students will also be able to evaluate the appropriateness of different experimental designs in biological research, design experiments to answer specific questions, and work through analytic workflows of medium complexity.
The course runs in three modules — see the full Schedule for week-by-week topics:

R Crash Course (Weeks 1–3) — introduction to R, data management best practices, and the typical analytic workflow for experimental work in the life sciences.
Data Exploration (Weeks 4–6) — working with data in R, focused on summarizing and visualizing key characteristics of biological data.
Statistical Analysis and Interpretation (Weeks 7–14) — commonly used experimental designs and the statistical techniques typically used to analyze biological data, pairing fundamental principles with applied practice each week.

title: Syllabus
text:
Learning objectives
At the end of this course, students will be able to:

Apply principles of data management and project organization to facilitate the analysis of experimental data.
Use the R coding language to import, clean, analyze, and visualize experimental data.
Produce robust exploratory data analyses and visualizations for commonly encountered experimental designs.
Discuss the appropriateness of different statistical tests for various experimental designs.
Interpret the results of key statistical analyses.

Academic integrity policy
All students are advised of the university policy on academic integrity. Academic honesty is essential to maintaining trust in the learning environment and ensuring all students are evaluated fairly. Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their own work; academic dishonesty in any form (plagiarism, cheating, fabrication, facilitating dishonesty) will not be tolerated and may result in disciplinary action, up to and including failure of the assignment or course, and referral to the provost’s office.






ImportantAI statement



You are strongly discouraged from the use of AI and LLM agents (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) in this course. While some uses — like proofreading written assignments or brainstorming ideas — can be beneficial, an increasingly common observation is that use of AI tools when learning new techniques (and especially when learning to code) blocks the development of skills and understanding.
Any AI usage must be documented in detail, and students must be able to describe how generated output was modified to reflect their own thoughts and perspective. Students are encouraged to think about (1) the consequences of AI usage for their own learning and for the environment, and (2) how AI use affects the development of critical thinking skills. As a general rule, assignments generated entirely or primarily by AI will not be accepted. In the event of suspected AI-generated responses, Dr. Sasaki may choose to check student understanding via a conversation and discuss how the answer was arrived at. After an initial warning, however, violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct, subject to the university’s Academic Integrity procedures.

title: Syllabus
text:
Assignments
Over the course of the semester, you will complete a range of Assignments meant to develop your understanding of key points from the lecture materials. These assignments fall into three general categories:
Problem Sets – Students will complete weekly coding problem sets, questions about concepts and theory with application in both hypothetical and real-world scenarios. When analyzing example data sets, students will be asked to describe the methods and interpret results, as might be required when preparing scientific publications. Problem sets are graded on completion.
Data Safari Exercises – In these exercises, students are tasked to replicate a figure from the published literature using the publicly available data from that study. Students will also be asked to reflect on the process for each exercise: How easy was it to follow the published methods? How well does your plot match the published version? How would you change the paper, plot, or data to improve reproducibility?
Projects – In addition to the above components, graduate students are required to complete a project over the course of the semester. These projects will be broken down into the main analytic steps we will cover in this course – experimental design and planned hypothesis testing, data carpentry and exploration, statistical modelling, and visualization. Ideally, students will complete this project using their own data, but data obtained from the published literature is also acceptable. Projects will be presented at the end of the semester.
Assignments are distributed as Quarto (.qmd) templates, downloadable from the Schedule. Complete them in the template, then render to PDF (via Typst, bundled with Quarto) and submit both the .qmd and the .pdf. Given the pacing and breadth of this course, it is important to turn work in on time. Late assignments can be turned in for credit up to three weeks following the deadline, but will be docked 2% for every day past the due date (weekends included).

When parametric tests break down
Recall from Labs 4–6: t-tests, ANOVA, and regression all assume roughly normal, equal-variance residuals. When sample sizes are small and that assumption clearly fails (e.g., strongly skewed data, extreme outliers you can’t justify removing), nonparametric methods based on ranks are a safer choice.

title: Week 13 Tutorial: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Crossed vs. nested random effects

Nested: each level of one factor only occurs within one level of another (e.g., plot within site — plot 1 at Site A is a different physical plot than plot 1 at Site B). Write as (1 | site/plot).
Crossed: levels of one factor occur across multiple levels of another (e.g., the same observer measures animals at multiple sites). Write as (1 | site) + (1 | observer).







NoteExercise 2



You measure lizard body condition at 5 sites, with 3 plots per site (plots are physically distinct per site), and each plot is visited by one of 2 rotating observers who each work across multiple sites. Write the lmer() random-effects structure you’d use, and explain in one sentence why each grouping factor is crossed or nested.








NoteExercise 3



Look back at Week 5’s tutorial on blocking. A randomized block design and a mixed model with (1 | block) are closely related ideas — both treat block-to-block variation as a nuisance to control for rather than a treatment to test. In 2–3 sentences, explain the connection in your own words.

section: Why not just use lm()? Pseudoreplication revisited
text:
Why not just use lm()? Pseudoreplication revisited

set.seed(21)
n_sites <- 8
n_per_site <- 6

field_data <- tibble(site = factor(rep(1:n_sites, each = n_per_site))) |>
  mutate(
    site_effect = rep(rnorm(n_sites, 0, 3), each = n_per_site),
    treatment = rep(rep(c("Control", "Treated"), n_per_site / 2), n_sites),
    response = 10 + ifelse(treatment == "Treated", 2, 0) +
      site_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

Measurements within the same site aren’t independent — they share a site effect. Ignoring that (treating all 48 rows as independent) inflates your effective sample size and your false-positive rate.

m_naive <- lm(response ~ treatment, data = field_data)
summary(m_naive)$coefficients

title: Week 11 Tutorial: Logistic Regression and GLMs
text:
Why not just use lm()?
A linear model fit to a 0/1 outcome can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1, and violates the constant-variance assumption near the extremes. Logistic regression models the log-odds of the outcome instead.

title: Week 6 Tutorial: Design in Practice
section: A framework for reading a methods section
text:
A framework for reading a methods section
Whenever you read the methods of a paper, try to answer these questions, in this order:

What is the experimental unit? The thing that was independently assigned to a treatment — not necessarily the thing that was measured (recall Week 5’s pseudoreplication discussion).
What are the treatments/groups, and how many levels does each factor have?
How many experimental units per treatment (the replication)?
Was assignment to treatment randomized? If so, how — and if not, is it an observational study instead?
Was there any blocking, matching, or other control for a known source of variation?
What was the response variable, and how was it measured?
What statistical test or model did the authors use to analyze it — and does that choice match the design (matching what we covered in Weeks 5 and 7 onward)?

title: Week 6 Tutorial: Design in Practice
text:
Worked example (hypothetical)
Consider a hypothetical study: researchers want to know whether a soil amendment increases seedling survival in a restoration planting. They have 40 plots across a hillside, and randomly assign half to receive the amendment and half to serve as controls. Survival is recorded after one growing season.
Applying the framework:

Experimental unit: the plot (not the individual seedling — seedlings within a plot share soil and microclimate, so they aren’t independent).
Treatments: one factor, two levels (amendment vs. control).
Replication: 20 plots per treatment.
Randomization: yes — amendment assigned randomly across plots.
Blocking: none mentioned; if the hillside has a known elevation gradient, that’s a missed opportunity to block.
Response variable: proportion of seedlings surviving per plot.
Analysis: a logistic regression or a t-test on arcsine-transformed proportions would both be defensible choices here — this connects to Week 11’s lecture on the logistic alternative to lm().

section: Simulating a randomized complete block design
text:
Simulating a randomized complete block design
Suppose greenhouse bench position affects plant growth independent of treatment. A randomized block design assigns each treatment once per bench (block), so bench-to-bench variation can be separated from treatment effects.

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)


n_blocks <- 6
treatments <- c("Control", "Low_N", "High_N")

design <- expand_grid(block = factor(1:n_blocks), treatment = treatments)

block_effect <- rnorm(n_blocks, mean = 0, sd = 3)
names(block_effect) <- levels(design$block)

design <- design |>
  mutate(
    trt_effect = case_when(
      treatment == "Control" ~ 0,
      treatment == "Low_N"   ~ 2,
      treatment == "High_N"  ~ 5
    ),
    growth = 20 + trt_effect + block_effect[as.character(block)] +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

title: Why Experimental Design Matters

A question to sit with

If you ran the same experiment twice, would you trust the second result as much as the first?


A good design makes the answer “yes”

title: Why Experimental Design Matters
text:
Why design comes before analysis

No statistical test can fix a poorly designed study
Common failure modes we’ll dissect this semester:

Pseudoreplication (measuring the same unit many times, treating it as many replicates)
Confounding (treatment tangled up with some other variable)
Underpowered studies (too few replicates to detect a real effect)

title: Why Experimental Design Matters
text:
A biology example

Question: does a fertilizer increase plant growth?

We’ll spend Weeks 5–6 building the vocabulary to catch this

title: Exploring Distributions

Why explore before modeling?

Every statistical test we’ll cover assumes something about your data (roughly normal, similar variance across groups, no wild outliers)
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is how you check those assumptions before you’re deep into a model and it’s too late to notice

title: Exploring Distributions

What to look for

Skew: is the mean pulled away from the median?
Unequal spread: do groups have wildly different variances?
Outliers: are there points that don’t look like they belong?

Catching a problem now is far cheaper than debugging a confusing model result in six weeks

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
From exploring to designing

Weeks 1–4: get comfortable with R and with looking at data
Starting today: how do you make sure the data you collect can actually answer your question?

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Three pillars

Replication — measuring enough independent experimental units
Randomization — assigning treatments in a way that avoids bias
Blocking — controlling for a known source of variation you’re not interested in

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Replication: how many is enough?

More replicates → smaller standard errors → easier to detect a real effect
But replication means independent experimental units, not repeated measurements of the same unit
We’ll formalize “how many” with power analysis later in the course

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
The experimental unit, again

The thing that was independently assigned to a treatment
Not necessarily the thing you measured
Classic trap: 1 tank of 50 fish, “n = 50” — really n = 1 tank

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Pseudoreplication

Treating non-independent measurements as if they were independent replicates
Inflates your effective sample size
Inflates your false-positive rate — you’ll find “significant” effects that aren’t real

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Randomization

Protects against confounding: without it, treatment can get tangled up with some other variable (time of day, position, batch)
“I gave the healthiest-looking plants the new fertilizer” is not randomization — it’s a confound waiting to happen

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Blocking

Groups experimental units into blocks that share some nuisance variable (bench position, day, litter, site)
Assign every treatment once within each block
Lets you statistically remove block-to-block variation from your error term

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Blocking in action

Naive model: growth ~ treatment
Blocked model: growth ~ treatment + block
Blocking usually shrinks the residual variance, making it easier to detect the treatment effect — we’ll simulate this today

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
When blocking doesn’t help much

If the nuisance variable barely matters, blocking costs you degrees of freedom for little benefit
Worth checking, not assuming

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
This week

Wednesday (tutorial): simulate a randomized block design in R, compare naive vs. blocked models

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
Why this matters

Textbook examples are clean by design
Real papers bury the design in a paragraph of prose — you have to extract it yourself
This is a skill you’ll use for the rest of your career, not just this course

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
A framework: seven questions

What is the experimental unit?
What are the treatments, and how many levels?
How many experimental units per treatment?
Was assignment randomized?
Was there blocking or matching?
What was the response variable, and how was it measured?
Does the statistical analysis match the design?

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
Question 1 is the hardest

Not “how many measurements” — “how many independently assigned units”
If you’re unsure, ask: what would it mean to have one more replicate here?

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
A worked example

Hypothetical: soil amendment vs. seedling survival, 40 plots, 20 per treatment, randomly assigned
Experimental unit: the plot (not the individual seedling)
Randomization: yes. Blocking: none — and the hillside likely has an elevation gradient that could have been blocked on

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
What “no blocking” costs you

Not necessarily wrong — just possibly less powerful than it could have been
Part of your job as a reader (and later, a designer) is spotting missed opportunities like this

Apply the seven-question framework

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
section: From design to your first test
text:
From design to your first test

Weeks 5–6: design principles, and finding them in the literature
Today: your first formal hypothesis test — connecting a design to the right analysis

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
The simplest case: two groups

Comparing a numeric outcome between exactly two groups
The tool: t.test()
Paired or unpaired? Depends on your design — measurements from the same subject under two conditions are paired

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
Three or more groups: ANOVA

Comparing means across 3+ groups
The tool: aov()
Null hypothesis: all group means are equal
A significant ANOVA tells you some group differs — not which

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
Checking assumptions

Residuals roughly normal (Q-Q plot)
Similar variance across groups (Levene’s test, residuals-vs-fitted plot)
These are exactly the checks Weeks 3–4 trained you to make

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
section: After a significant ANOVA: post-hoc tests
text:
After a significant ANOVA: post-hoc tests

emmeans() + pairs() for pairwise comparisons
Correct for multiple comparisons (Tukey) — testing many pairs inflates your false-positive rate

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
From test back to design

A test only tells you what to do with data you already have
The design determines whether the data can answer your question at all
Example: 3 fertilizer doses, 1 greenhouse, 18 pots — what’s the experimental unit? How would you randomize?

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
This week

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
Welcome back

Spring Break’s over — quick recap: t-tests and ANOVA compare group means
Today: what if both variables are continuous?

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
Correlation

cor() / cor.test() — strength and direction of a linear relationship, summarized in a single number (−1 to 1)
Says nothing about why two things move together

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
Simple linear regression

lm(y ~ x) — models y as a straight-line function of x
Gives you a slope (effect size), not just a correlation coefficient
tidy() and glance() (from broom) for clean summaries

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
Checking the fit

Residuals vs. fitted — is the relationship actually linear?
Q-Q plot — are residuals roughly normal?
R² — how much variance does the model explain?

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
section: Correlation and regression are not causation
text:
Correlation and regression are not causation

trees: girth predicts volume — but nobody assigned girth
This is observational data
Contrast with Week 7, where treatment was randomly assigned — there, a significant result supports a causal claim

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
Design still matters here

A strong, statistically significant regression from observational data still can’t prove causation
If you want to claim causation, you need an experiment — random assignment of the predictor, not just measurement of it

title: Correlation and Linear Regression
text:
This week

Wednesday (tutorial): fit and check a simple linear regression, compare correlation vs. regression
Assignment: due this week

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
From one predictor to several

Last week: y ~ x, one continuous predictor
Real biological outcomes usually depend on more than one thing at once

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
Multiple regression

lm(y ~ x1 + x2) — each coefficient is the effect of that predictor holding the others constant
Compare models with anova(model_simple, model_full) — does adding a predictor meaningfully improve the fit?

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
ANCOVA: mixing categorical and continuous

One categorical predictor (treatment) + one continuous covariate (e.g., starting size)
lm(final ~ start + treatment)
The treatment coefficient is the group difference after accounting for the covariate

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
Why control for the covariate?

Without it: a group difference in final_height might just reflect a group difference in start_height, not a true treatment effect
With it: you’re comparing groups on a level playing field

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
Checking for an interaction

ANCOVA assumes parallel slopes across groups
lm(final ~ start * treatment) tests whether that assumption holds
A significant interaction means the treatment effect depends on the covariate — a more interesting (and more complex) story

title: Multiple Regression and ANCOVA
text:
Connecting back to design

This is Experimental Designs III territory: multiple predictors mean your design needs to consider more than one source of variation
A covariate you didn’t measure is a covariate you can’t control for

title: Logistic Regression and Other GLMs
text:
When lm() breaks down

lm() assumes a continuous, roughly normal outcome
What about survival (yes/no)? Count of offspring? Number of parasites?

title: Logistic Regression and Other GLMs
text:
Logistic regression

For binary outcomes (survived/died, germinated/didn’t)
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)
Models the log-odds of the outcome, not the outcome directly
Exponentiate coefficients to get odds ratios — more interpretable

title: Logistic Regression and Other GLMs
text:
Poisson regression

For count outcomes (number of offspring, number of parasites)
glm(y ~ x, family = poisson)
Watch for overdispersion: if the residual deviance is much larger than the residual df, consider quasi-Poisson or negative binomial instead

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
section: A problem we’ve flagged since Week 5
text:
A problem we’ve flagged since Week 5

Pseudoreplication: measurements within the same site/subject/plot aren’t independent
Ignoring this inflates your effective sample size and false-positive rate
Today: a proper tool for handling it, instead of just avoiding it

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Random vs. fixed effects

Fixed effect: a variable whose specific levels you care about (e.g., treatment)
Random effect: a grouping variable representing a sample from a larger population of possible groups (e.g., site, subject)

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
The random-intercept model

lmer(response ~ treatment + (1 | site), data = ...)
Lets each site have its own baseline, while estimating one shared treatment effect
Standard errors on fixed effects usually get larger and more honest once you do this correctly

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
section: Why not just add site as a fixed effect?
text:
Why not just add site as a fixed effect?

You could — but then you’re estimating a separate parameter for every site, and can’t generalize beyond the specific sites you sampled
A random effect treats site as a sample from a broader population, which is usually what you actually want to say

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Connecting back to blocking

A randomized block design (Week 5) and (1 | block) are close cousins — both treat block-to-block variation as a nuisance to control for, not a treatment to test
Mixed models generalize this idea beyond simple block designs

title: Accounting for Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
A practical limit

Random effects need enough groups to estimate their variance reliably — as a rule of thumb, 5–10 groups minimum
With very few groups, consider a fixed effect instead

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Last week vs. this week

Last week: random intercepts — each group gets its own baseline
This week: what if the effect itself varies by group, and what happens with more complex grouping structures?

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Random slopes

lmer(response ~ treatment + (treatment | site), data = ...)
Lets the treatment effect itself vary from site to site
Compare to the random-intercept-only model with anova() — does allowing varying slopes meaningfully improve the fit?

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Nested random effects

One factor’s levels only make sense within another (e.g., plot within site — “plot 1” at Site A isn’t the same physical plot as “plot 1” at Site B)
Syntax: (1 | site/plot)

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Crossed random effects

Levels of one factor occur across multiple levels of another (e.g., the same observer measures animals at several sites)
Syntax: (1 | site) + (1 | observer)

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Telling them apart

Ask: does “level 1” mean the same thing across every group?

Yes → crossed
No → nested

Getting this wrong doesn’t always error — it silently gives you the wrong model

title: Mixed-Effects Models II: Slopes, Crossed, and Nested Designs
text:
Putting it together

Design (Weeks 5–6) → naive vs. blocked model (Week 5) → mixed model with random intercepts (Week 12) → random slopes and crossed/nested structures (today)
Same underlying idea the whole way: account for the structure in how your data were collected

title: Nonparametric Alternatives and Choosing the Right Test

When parametric tests break down

Small sample size and clear evidence of non-normality or extreme outliers you can’t justify removing
Nonparametric tests, based on ranks rather than raw values, are a safer choice in that situation

A general-purpose backup: permutation tests

Build a null distribution directly from your own data by shuffling group labels
Useful when no standard nonparametric test fits your specific design
More computationally intensive, but conceptually simple

title: Nonparametric Alternatives and Choosing the Right Test
section: Choosing a test: the whole course in one slide

Choosing a test: the whole course in one slide

What type is your outcome? (continuous, binary, count)
How many groups / predictors?
Are your residuals reasonably normal, with similar variance across groups?
Is there any non-independence (repeated measures, nesting) you need to account for?
If assumptions are badly violated and nothing else fits — consider a nonparametric or permutation-based approach
